questions.question: If a lattice basis is perfectly orthogonal, what does CVP reduce to for integer targets?
options: Independent rounding of each coordinate in the orthogonal basis
Solving a shortest vector problem (SVP) in the dual lattice
Running LLL until the determinant decreases
Enumerating all integer combinations in a coefficient window
questions.explanation: With an orthogonal basis, the Voronoi cell is an axis-aligned box in that coordinate system, so rounding each coordinate gives a closest lattice point.

questions.question: What does Gram–Schmidt produce from a basis b1,...,bn that Babai/LLL rely on?
options: Orthogonal vectors b* plus projection coefficients μ
A unimodular matrix U with det(U)=±1
A shortest non-zero lattice vector
A factorization of the determinant into primes
questions.explanation: Gram–Schmidt gives orthogonal b* vectors and projection coefficients μ that describe how basis vectors project onto earlier directions.

questions.question: In Babai’s nearest-plane algorithm, in what order do you process the basis directions?
options: From the last Gram–Schmidt direction down to the first
From the first basis vector up to the last
In an arbitrary order; it does not matter
Only the shortest basis vector is used
questions.explanation: Babai rounds the coefficient along b*_n, subtracts, then continues with b*_{n-1}, and so on down to b*_1.

questions.question: What quantity does Babai round at step i (using the Gram–Schmidt data)?
options: <residual, b*_i> / <b*_i, b*_i>
<residual, b_i> / <b_i, b_i>
questions.explanation: Babai rounds the coordinate of the residual along the orthogonal direction b*_i: <r,b*_i>/<b*_i,b*_i>.

questions.question: Why do we typically run LLL (or BKZ) before Babai in practical workflows?
options: Babai’s quality depends strongly on basis orthogonality; reduction makes the basis less skew
Babai requires the determinant to be 1, and LLL enforces that
Babai only works when all basis vectors have the same length, which LLL guarantees
LLL converts CVP into an exact SVP instance
questions.explanation: Babai is basis-dependent; reducing the basis usually improves Gram–Schmidt geometry, making the rounding decisions more reliable.

questions.question: Which failure mode best explains how Babai can return a non-optimal lattice vector on a skew basis?
options: An early rounding decision sends the residual to the wrong affine coset, and later steps cannot recover
The lattice stops being discrete when the basis is skew
Gram–Schmidt only works for prime determinants
Babai always solves exact CVP, so it cannot fail
questions.explanation: On a skew basis, rounding along b*_i can choose the wrong hyperplane; the remaining steps only search within that choice.

questions.question: Why does the lesson implement Gram–Schmidt with exact Fractions instead of floats?
options: To avoid numerical noise that can flip ‘round to nearest integer’ decisions
Because floats cannot represent integers at all
Because Fractions are asymptotically faster than floats
Because LLL/Babai require constant-time arithmetic
questions.explanation: Babai/LLL depend on comparisons to 1/2 and nearest-integer rounding; small floating errors can change decisions on integer inputs.

questions.question: In a bounded-distance decoding (BDD) setting, what is the typical role of Babai’s output?
options: A fast candidate that is often correct when the target is sufficiently close to the lattice
A proof that the basis is unimodular
A way to compute the exact smoothing parameter
A method to factor the determinant
questions.explanation: BDD assumes the target is near the lattice; with a reduced basis, Babai frequently returns the intended nearest lattice vector.
